steps.title: Rosé
steps.body: Cinsault's thin skins, low tannin and fresh red fruit make it ideal for rosé. It gives pale colour fast, with strawberry and floral notes. In Provence, it's a key partner to Grenache in pale, dry rosé. Tavel and Languedoc rosés use it too.

steps.title: South Africa
steps.body: Cinsault, called Hermitage there in the past, was South Africa's most planted red grape until the 1970s, used for bulk wine and brandy. In 1925, Abraham Perold crossed it with Pinot Noir to create Pinotage. Today, young producers make fresh, light Cinsault from old bush vines, a revival of a forgotten grape.
steps.highlight: Parent of Pinotage, revived from old vines

steps.prompt: Which grape did Perold create by crossing Cinsault with Pinot Noir?

steps.title: Old vines
steps.body: South Africa's Old Vine Project certifies vineyards over 35 years old, many of them Cinsault. Some, in Wellington and Darling, were planted in the early 20th century. Their low yields give concentration to a grape known for lightness. The wines are pale yet complex.

steps.prompt: In South Africa, Cinsault was once called ____.
steps.explanation: Hence the name Pinotage, from Pinot plus Hermitage.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cinsault's thin skins make it ideal for rosé
It's a parent of Pinotage, created in 1925
South Africa's old Cinsault vines are being revived
